units.translation: Apollonius, then, says that Heracles was left behind near Cius after disembarking to search for Hylas; but Dionysius of Mytilene (32 F 6b J.) says that the hero sailed with the chiefs as far as Colchis and accomplished the business concerning Medea together with Jason. Similarly also Demaretes (42 F 2b J.). But Herodorus (31 F 41b J.) says that he and certain others did not sail with them. Hesiod in the Marriage of Ceyx (fr. 154 Rz.²) says that he disembarked to search for water in Magnesia and was left behind near the place called Aphetae from his departure. But Antimachus in the Lyde (fr. 8 B. II 290) says that Heracles was put ashore because the Argo was weighed down by the hero 〈...〉 and Poseidippus the epigrammatist (fr. 4 Schott, Posid. epigr., Diss. Berol. 1907, 106) followed, and Pherecydes (3 F 111b J.). But Ephorus in the fifth book (70 F 14b J.) says that he was left behind voluntarily to go to Omphale, queen of the Lydians. But Anticleides in the second book of the Deliaca (140 F 2 J.) says that Hyllus, the son of Heracles, disembarked for water and did not return.

He does not mention the urgent occasion, but refers the speech to the return, in order to reproach the deed more; for it made no difference to you to be defeated by Heracles in Scythia, but nevertheless this brought shame upon you later when we returned to Greece. Therefore you also abandoned the common safety of all for the sake of your own glory.

But what pleasure is there in words: Herodian in the twentieth book (I 537, 11 L.) says that disyllabic neuter nouns ending in -ος, beginning with a naturally long vowel, have a smooth breathing: αἶσχος, ἦθος, εὖρος, εἶδος. Thus also ἦδος. But ἡθμός is aspirated, although it has η before θ in meaning, because the future ἥσω is aspirated. But μοί is missing. For the sense is: but what pleasure is there for me in these words? For I will go apart from this deceit that has been arranged for you.
